This is a reduction of the configured exercise, including its disclosed support interpretation. Its hypotheses are exactly the original ones: integers n,m≥1; a jointly C∞ map on ℝⁿ×(0,∞); a fixed Euclidean unit vector q; unit length of u; pointwise normality of u_tt−Δu with a merely existential real scalar at each point; and for every 0<s<t a compact spatial C_[s,t] outside which u=q throughout [s,t]. No regularity of that scalar, initial data, common compact set for all positive times, or support assumption on u itself is added. The required conclusion includes integrability and differentiability of the finite integral as well as its zero derivative.

1. Coordinate representation (part of B010).
Identify ℝⁿ and ℝᵐ with functions on Fin n and Fin m in their fixed standard coordinates. Use canonical Lebesgue volume on Fin n→ℝ, which is the product of the usual one-dimensional Lebesgue measures. This is the given dx, with no Jacobian, normalization factor or change of basis. On the finite coordinate spaces the product norm topology agrees with the Euclidean topology; differentiability and C∞ regularity are therefore the original ones. Define dot(v,w)=∑_k v_k w_k and normSq(v)=dot(v,v). In particular normSq is the Euclidean norm squared, regardless of the norm used for the ambient Lean function type. Thus normSq q=1 and UnitValued express exactly the original unit constraints, not a supremum norm constraint. Extend u arbitrarily to t≤0, for example by q there, solely to give total Lean functions. The open set U={(x,t):0<t} contains all points where any assertion is made. Smooth means ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ on U, not analyticity, and imposes no regularity on this extension at zero. Restriction of a total representative and arbitrary extension give both directions of the representation of the original half-space map. Derivatives at positive times are local and hence independent of the extension.

The header defines V=u_t, A=u_tt, P_j=∂_j u, S_j=∂_jj u, L=∑_j S_j, e=dot(V,V)+∑_j dot(P_j,P_j), E(t)=∫ e(x,t) dx. All component derivatives use ordinary real deriv or fderiv evaluated at the standard vector e_j=Pi.single j 1. In particular L is exactly the componentwise Laplacian, and e uses the Frobenius square with coefficient 1 on both terms. The header's Normal and CompactPerturbation are precisely the pointwise scalar equation and the quantified slab support hypothesis. This representation changes no original assumption or conclusion. In what follows all times under discussion lie strictly above zero.

2. Smooth calculus and mixed derivatives (B010, using B004, B005, B006).
Let w(x,t)=u(x,t)_k be one scalar coordinate, p=(x,t), T=(0,1) and X_j=(e_j,0). Scalar projection is a continuous linear map, so w is C∞ on U. The derivative of the affine time section r↦(x,r) is h↦(0,h); the derivative of y↦(y,t) is h↦(h,0). The chain rule therefore identifies V_k(p)=Dw(p)T and P_j,k(p)=Dw(p)X_j. These follow as HasDerivAt/HasFDerivAt statements first, followed by uniqueness of derivatives. Apply B006 on U, then evaluate at the fixed vector T or X_j, to see that these functions are again C∞ on U. Repeating B006 gives all the second derivatives and the regularity claimed here. These steps use only composition with continuous linear maps, the ordinary chain rule, and smoothness on an open domain.

For precision put H_p(v,w)=D(Dw)(p)(v)(w). Differentiating the fixed evaluations gives ∂_t P_j,k=H_p(T,X_j), ∂_j V_k=H_p(X_j,T), A_k=H_p(T,T) and S_j,k=H_p(X_j,X_j). B005, applied to the C² scalar w at p, says H_p(T,X_j)=H_p(X_j,T). Thus put W_j,k=∂_j V_k=∂_t P_j,k; this is an equality of actual derivatives of the functions already defined, not an additional PDE assumption. Each quantity and W_j is C∞ on U. Applying B004 to a scalar function multiplied by itself gives derivative 2f f'; differentiating finite coordinate sums and then the finite spatial sum yields
 d(x,t) := 2 dot(V(x,t),A(x,t)) + 2∑_j dot(P_j(x,t),W_j(x,t)),
 HasDerivAt (r↦e(x,r)) d(x,t) t.
Finite sums and products also show d is C∞ on U. This proves B010. The basic finite-sum, linear-map and chain-rule steps are ordinary internal calculus, with the whole pinned Mathlib available for their eventual Lean proofs; the prepared basis is not a restriction on theorem use.

3. Slab support and integrability (B011, using B001, B007, B010).
Fix any t₀>0. The original compactness hypothesis with s=t₀/2 and t=3t₀/2 is applicable since 0<t₀/2<3t₀/2. Choose its compact C and write J=[t₀/2,3t₀/2], I=(t₀/2,3t₀/2). A compact subset of the finite-dimensional real coordinate space is closed. Therefore O=Cᶜ×I is open. On O the original hypothesis says u=q. Around each point of O each scalar coordinate of u equals a constant on a neighborhood. B007 makes its Fréchet derivative zero. This equality holds throughout O, so the same locality argument applied again to that zero derivative makes the next derivatives zero. Inducting proves vanishing of all positive-order derivatives on O. Evaluating the spacetime derivatives in the directions in paragraph 2 gives V=A=P_j=S_j=W_j=0 there. In particular e and d vanish there.

For each r∈I, all of these quantities have continuous spatial sections by B010. Each displayed scalar section vanishes off C. Its ordinary support is therefore contained in C, and so is its closure because C is closed. Hence it has compact topological support. The same assertions hold for any finite sum or product of these sections, in particular V_k A_k, P_j,k W_j,k, V_k S_j,k, V_k P_j,k, W_j,k P_j,k, all their dot products and all finite sums used below. B001 makes every such scalar function integrable with respect to volume, and makes e(·,r) and d(·,r) integrable. This is also absolute integrability because these are real Bochner integrals. Taking r=t₀ and allowing arbitrary t₀>0 proves that the energy density is integrable at every requested time. Nothing about derivative vanishing at the time endpoints of J is asserted or needed.

4. Differentiation of the actual integral (B012, using B002, B008, B009, B010, B011).
Set η=t₀/4>0, K_t=[t₀−η,t₀+η] and s_t=(t₀−η,t₀+η). Direct inequalities from t₀>0 show K_t⊂I and s_t is a neighborhood of t₀. The product C×K_t is compact and lies in U. Continuity of d on this product and B008 give B₀ with |d(x,r)|≤B₀ for (x,r) in it. Put B=max(B₀,0) and b(x)=C.indicator(fun _↦B)(x). B009 makes b integrable. For x∈C and r∈s_t the compact bound gives |d(x,r)|≤b(x). For x∉C the left side is zero by paragraph 3 and the right side is zero. Thus for every spatial x, for every r∈s_t, the bound holds. In particular, the entire predicate (∀ r∈s_t, |d(x,r)|≤b(x)) holds for Lebesgue-almost every x. This is exactly the ae-first order required by B002; the exceptional set can be empty. This argument also handles C=∅ without choosing a maximum point.

Apply B002 with F(r,x)=e(x,r), F'(r,x)=d(x,r), basepoint t₀, neighborhood s_t, bound b. Here are all its hypotheses: s_t∈𝓝 t₀ as above; for all r∈s_t the spatial section e(·,r) is continuous and therefore ae strongly measurable, giving the required eventual measurability; e(·,t₀) is integrable by paragraph 3; d(·,t₀) is continuous and therefore ae strongly measurable; the bound hypothesis is ∀ᵐ x ∂volume, ∀ r∈s_t, |d(x,r)|≤b(x), obtained by applying ae_of_all volume to the universal-in-r predicate established in the preceding cases; b is integrable by B009; and for every spatial x, for every r∈s_t, paragraph 2 gives HasDerivAt (s↦e(x,s)) d(x,r) r because r>0. A second application of ae_of_all volume to this universal-in-r derivative predicate supplies ∀ᵐ x ∂volume, ∀ r∈s_t, HasDerivAt (s↦e(x,s)) d(x,r) r. These are the exact quantifier orders in B002's native theorem and prepared Lean proposition. Both hold everywhere in x, with no time-dependent spatial exceptional sets. B002 concludes
 HasDerivAt E (∫ x, d(x,t₀)) t₀.
This proves differentiability of the original finite integral, rather than merely writing a formal derivative of an integral. The compact bound is local in t₀ and C, as allowed by the original hypotheses; it is not a new uniform bound on u over the whole half-space.

5. Tangency and the normality cancellation (B013, using B004, B010).
For fixed x, the unit constraint says ∑_k u_k(x,r)²=1 for every r>0. It therefore agrees locally with the constant 1 around every t>0. By B004 and the first derivative statements of paragraph 2, the derivative of this sum is 2∑_k u_k(x,t)V_k(x,t). Uniqueness of the derivative of a constant gives 2 dot(u,V)=0, hence dot(u,V)=0. Commutativity of real multiplication gives dot(V,u)=0. At just this (x,t), take a witness a from the original normality assumption A−L=a u. Finite-sum distributivity gives
 dot(V,A−L)=dot(V,a u)=a dot(V,u)=0.
No function selecting all witnesses is needed. In particular there is no continuity assumption on a and no differentiation of a. The supplied proof's optional explicit formula for a and its twice-differentiated constraint are unnecessary and are removed from the active proof.

6. Spatial integration by parts (B014, using B003, B010, B011).
Fix t₀>0, j∈Fin n and k∈Fin m. On the entire spatial coordinate space define f(x)=V_k(x,t₀) and g(x)=P_j,k(x,t₀), and take v=e_j. B010 makes f and g smooth, hence differentiable everywhere and in particular on the respective topological supports required by B003. Their directional derivatives are Df(x)e_j=W_j,k(x,t₀) and Dg(x)e_j=S_j,k(x,t₀). Each of (Df e_j)g, f(Dg e_j), and fg is continuous with compact support and integrable by paragraph 3. Thus every hypothesis of B003 is satisfied, giving
 ∫ x, V_k S_j,k = −∫ x, W_j,k P_j,k.
Sum over the finitely many k. The individual summands are integrable, so linearity commutes the sum and integral. Commuting real products inside the right integrand and changing the sign gives
 ∫ x, dot(P_j,W_j) = −∫ x, dot(V,S_j).
This is exactly the integration-by-parts identity used in the supplied proof, obtained directly from native whole-space integration by parts. No box-boundary or unproved multidimensional divergence theorem is introduced.

7. Assembly and normalization (B015, using B011–B014).
At the arbitrary t₀>0, paragraph 4 gives the derivative ∫ d. All of the following integral algebra has the integrability hypotheses from paragraph 3: finite sums, dot-product expansions, products, real scalar multiples and differences. Substitute the definition of d, then paragraph 6 for every j:
 ∫ d = 2∫ dot(V,A) + 2∑_j∫ dot(P_j,W_j)
      = 2∫ dot(V,A) − 2∑_j∫ dot(V,S_j)
      = 2∫ dot(V,A−∑_j S_j)
      = 2∫ dot(V,A−L) = 0.
The last equality is pointwise paragraph 5 followed by the integral of zero. Rewriting the derivative statement of paragraph 4 now gives HasDerivAt E 0 t₀. This includes differentiability and E'(t₀)=0. Paragraph 3 separately gives integrability at t₀. Since t₀>0 was arbitrary, all three requested conclusions hold at every positive time, with exactly coefficient 1 on |u_t|² and on each spatial derivative square. This establishes the full selected target; the usual constancy formulation of conservation is also a consequence of the zero derivative on the interval (0,∞). No assertion at time zero or altered PDE is used.

A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.

1: # Conservation of energy for a sphere-valued wave map
2: 
3: ## Original exercise
4: 
5: Lawrence C. Evans, *Partial Differential Equations*, second edition,
6: Graduate Studies in Mathematics 19, AMS, 2010, section 12.6, exercise 14,
7: printed page 694. The preceding exercise 13 defines the sphere-valued
8: wave map. ISBN: 978-0-8218-4974-3.
9: 
10: > 14. Prove that if \(\mathbf u\) is a wave map into the unit sphere,
11: > with compact support in space, we have conservation of energy:
12: > \[
13: > \frac{d}{dt}\int_{\mathbb R^n}
14: >       |\mathbf u_t|^2+|D\mathbf u|^2\,dx=0.
15: > \]
16: 
17: ## Fixed interpretation and complete target
18: 
19: A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
20: the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
21: of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
22: This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
23: correction.
24: 
25: Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
26: \(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
27: Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:
28: 
29: 1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
30: 2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
31:    \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
32:    \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
33:    assumed.
34: 3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
35:    \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
36:    \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).
37: 
38: With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define
39: 
40: \[
41: e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
42: \qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
43: \]
44: 
45: The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
46: \(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
47: Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
48: and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
49: 
50: ## Fixed natural-language proof
51: 
52: ### 1. Tangency and the wave-map equation
53: 
54: Differentiate \(u\cdot u=1\) in time. The product rule gives
55: \(2u\cdot u_t=0\), so
56: 
57: \[
58: u\cdot u_t=0,\qquad
59: u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)=a(u_t\cdot u)=0.          \tag{1}
60: \]
61: 
62: No derivative of \(a\) is needed. The familiar explicit equation also
63: follows from the assumptions: twice differentiating the unit constraint
64: gives \(u\cdot u_{tt}=-|u_t|^2\) and
65: \(u\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u=-|\partial_{x_j}u|^2\).
66: Dotting the normality equation with \(u\), using \(|u|^2=1\), yields
67: \(a=\sum_j|\partial_{x_j}u|^2-|u_t|^2\). This is a consequence,
68: not an additional PDE assumption.
69: 
70: ### 2. Common compact support and integrability
71: 
72: Fix \(t_0>0\), put \(J=[t_0/2,3t_0/2]\), and choose its compact
73: spatial set \(C\) from assumption 3. Since \(C\) is bounded, choose
74: \(R>0\) with \(C\subset(-R,R)^n\) and set \(Q=[-R,R]^n\).
75: The box has finite Lebesgue measure \((2R)^n\).
76: 
77: On the open set \((\mathbb R^n\setminus C)\times\operatorname{int}J\),
78: the map equals the constant \(q\), so all its positive-order
79: derivatives vanish. At interior times, \(e\), \(e_t\), and the
80: derivative products used below consequently vanish outside \(C\).
81: They are continuous by smoothness; their spatial sections are measurable,
82: bounded on \(Q\), and supported there. Their absolute integrals are
83: bounded by a finite constant times \(|Q|\). This proves integrability
84: of \(e(\cdot,t_0)\) and of all later terms. Since \(t_0\) was arbitrary,
85: the energy is a finite, well-defined integral at every positive time.
86: 
87: ### 3. Differentiate the energy integral
88: 
89: The product rule and equality of mixed derivatives give
90: 
91: \[
92: e_t=2u_t\cdot u_{tt}
93:    +2\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t.           \tag{2}
94: \]
95: 
96: Choose \(\eta>0\) so that
97: \([t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\subset\operatorname{int}J\).
98: Continuity of (2) on the compact box
99: \(Q\times[t_0-\eta,t_0+\eta]\) gives a finite bound \(|e_t|\leq B\).
100: For \(0<|h|<\eta\), the one-variable mean value theorem at fixed
101: \(x\) therefore gives
102: 
103: \[
104: \left|\frac{e(x,t_0+h)-e(x,t_0)}h\right|
105: \leq B\mathbf1_Q(x).
106: \]
107: 
108: Outside \(Q\), both densities vanish, so the bound holds throughout
109: \(\mathbb R^n\). The right side is integrable. The difference
110: quotients converge pointwise to \(e_t(x,t_0)\). Dominated convergence
111: and linearity for these integrable functions now prove
112: 
113: \[
114: E'(t_0)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e_t(x,t_0)\,dx.            \tag{3}
115: \]
116: 
117: This establishes differentiability of the actual finite integral.
118: 
119: ### 4. Integration by parts and cancellation
120: 
121: For each spatial index \(j\), at time \(t_0\) put
122: \(g_j(x)=u_t(x,t_0)\cdot\partial_{x_j}u(x,t_0)\).
123: It is smooth and vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of \(Q\),
124: because \(C\subset\operatorname{int}Q\). The product rule gives
125: 
126: \[
127: \partial_{x_j}g_j
128: =\partial_{x_j}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_j}u
129:  +u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u.
130: \]
131: 
132: Integrate first over \(x_j\in[-R,R]\) at fixed remaining coordinates.
133: The fundamental theorem of calculus gives zero because both endpoint
134: values of \(g_j\) are zero. Fubini applies on \(Q\) because the
135: derivative and its two summands are continuous and bounded on a
136: finite-measure box. Thus \(\int_Q\partial_{x_j}g_j=0\).
137: All these terms vanish outside \(Q\), so
138: 
139: \[
140: \int_{\mathbb R^n}\partial_{x_j}u\cdot\partial_{x_j}u_t\,dx
141: =-\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx.              \tag{4}
142: \]
143: 
144: Every integral is finite by step 2. Sum (4) over the finitely many
145: spatial indices and substitute (2) into (3):
146: 
147: \[
148: \begin{aligned}
149: E'(t_0)
150: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot u_{tt}\,dx
151:  -2\sum_{j=1}^n\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot\partial_{x_jx_j}u\,dx\\
152: &=2\int_{\mathbb R^n}u_t\cdot(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu)\,dx=0,
153: \end{aligned}
154: \]
155: 
156: by (1). This holds at every \(t_0>0\). Hence \(E\) is differentiable
157: with zero derivative on \((0,\infty)\), and is constant there by the
158: mean value theorem. This is conservation of energy with exactly the
159: normalization in the exercise.
160:

value.full_target:
A sphere-valued map cannot vanish outside a compact set. As approved by
the user on 2026-10-23, interpret spatial compact support as compact support
of a perturbation from a **fixed unit vector**, locally uniformly in time.
This is a disclosed nontrivial interpretation, not a claimed author-issued
correction.

Let \(n,m\geq1\) be integers and let
\(u:\mathbb R^n\times(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R^m\) be jointly smooth.
Fix \(q\in\mathbb R^m\) with \(|q|=1\). Assume:

1. \(|u(x,t)|=1\) for all \(x\) and \(t>0\).
2. The acceleration \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu\) is normal to the sphere at
   \(u\): at each point there is a real scalar \(a(x,t)\) with
   \(u_{tt}-\Delta_xu=a u\). No regularity of the selected scalar is
   assumed.
3. For every \(0<s<t<\infty\), a compact set
   \(C_{[s,t]}\subset\mathbb R^n\) exists such that \(u(x,r)=q\) for
   \(x\notin C_{[s,t]}\), \(r\in[s,t]\).

With Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure, define

\[
e(x,t)=|u_t(x,t)|^2+\sum_{j=1}^n|\partial_{x_j}u(x,t)|^2,
\qquad E(t)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}e(x,t)\,dx.
\]

The spatial gradient square is the Frobenius square, and
\(\Delta_xu=\sum_j\partial_{x_jx_j}u\) component by component.
Prove integrability of \(e(\cdot,t)\), differentiability of \(E\),
and \(E'(t)=0\) for every \(t>0\). No assertion at time zero is required.
value.conclusion: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝⁿ, the finite energy E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. Here e=|u_t|²+∑_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|² and E(t)=∫_{ℝⁿ}e(x,t) dx with Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure; there is no assertion at time zero.

definitions.type: notation for calculus, topology and measure
definitions.definition: AnalyticNotation fixes the following typed conventions, with each function, space, point and measure supplied by its own statement or local scope. D and fderiv denote the Fréchet derivative over the field specified at each use, defaulting to ℝ; deriv is the corresponding one-variable derivative. The total derivative operators return zero when a derivative does not exist. HasDerivAt relates a one-variable function, its derivative value and its basepoint. ContDiffOn and ContDiffAt express the indicated C-order regularity on a set or at a point; ∞ means all finite orders and ω means analytic. minSmoothness at order 2 is 2 for a field satisfying IsRCLikeNormedField and ω otherwise; IsSymmSndFDerivAt means that the second Fréchet derivative at the specified point is symmetric in its two direction arguments. 𝓝 denotes the neighborhood filter. The support of a function is the set where its value is nonzero, tsupport is the closure of that set, and HasCompactSupport means this closure is compact. ContinuousOn means continuity relative to the indicated set. AEStronglyMeasurable means agreement almost everywhere with a strongly measurable function. Integrable means ae strong measurability and finite integral of the norm; IntegrableOn means integrability with respect to the restriction of the specified measure to the specified set. The Bochner integral uses the total library convention; for real integrable functions it is the ordinary finite Lebesgue integral. A set indicator equals its function on that set and zero off it. An ae assertion holds outside a null set for the indicated measure. The extended norm on an ESeminormedAddMonoid is denoted by ‖·‖ₑ; real numbers have finite extended norm. Standard structure names retain their usual mathematical meanings: OpensMeasurableSpace says that open sets are measurable, BorelSpace identifies the measurable structure with the Borel structure, IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts says compact sets have finite measure, and IsAddHaarMeasure means an additive Haar measure. These conventions define notation and assert no application theorem.
V(x,t)_k=deriv (r↦ubar(x,r)_k) t, for each x,t and k∈Fin m.
A(x,t)_k=deriv (r↦V(x,r)_k) t.
Psp(j,x,t)_k=fderiv ℝ (y↦ubar(y,t)_k) x (basis(j)).
Ssp(j,x,t)_k=fderiv ℝ (y↦Psp(j,y,t)_k) x (basis(j)).
L(x,t)=∑_{j∈Fin n} Ssp(j,x,t), the componentwise spatial Laplacian.

dx is canonical Lebesgue volume on Space: the product of the usual real Lebesgue measures in its fixed standard coordinates. It is the original dx on ℝⁿ. Spatial integrals without a displayed measure use dx.
e(x,t)=normSq(V(x,t))+∑_{j∈Fin n} normSq(Psp(j,x,t)). This is |u_t|²+∑_j |∂_{x_j}u|² at positive times, with the Euclidean/Frobenius squares and coefficient 1 on each term.
E(t)=∫_{Space} e(x,t) dx, using the total integral convention until integrability is proved. At positive times when integrable this is the original finite energy integral.
W(j,x,t)_k=fderiv ℝ (y↦V(y,t)_k) x (basis(j)).
d(x,t)=2 dot(V(x,t),A(x,t))+2∑_{j∈Fin n} dot(Psp(j,x,t),W(j,x,t)).

argument.text: H001 fixes positive finite dimensions. Use the fixed standard coordinates on both original Euclidean spaces. For a vector in any such coordinate space, its maximum coordinate norm is at most its Euclidean norm, and its Euclidean norm is at most the square root of the number of coordinates times its maximum coordinate norm. Thus the coordinate identity and its inverse are continuous linear maps; they preserve Fréchet differentiability and all C∞ orders by the chain rule. The coordinates are the original standard ones, so dot and normSq are exactly the original dot product and squared Euclidean norm, not the product norm squared. Lebesgue measure in these standard coordinates is by definition the product of the usual real coordinate Lebesgue measures, giving dx with no Jacobian or rescaling. Restricting ubar to U recovers u, and conversely extension by q gives the total ubar. At a point of U a neighborhood stays in U, so all derivatives there are local and independent of the extension at nonpositive times. H002 therefore gives C∞ regularity of ubar on U. The derivative definitions, finite coordinate sums and the measure identification give the asserted meanings of V,A,Psp,Ssp,L,e,E once their actual derivative identities are checked below. Record F001: this coordinate representation, measure and norm identification is faithful, and ubar is C∞ on U.

produces.statement: The coordinate identities are continuous linear isomorphisms preserving the original Euclidean differential calculus; normSq is the Euclidean square and dx is the original Lebesgue measure. ubar restricted to U is u and ubar is C∞ on U. All derivatives at positive times are independent of the arbitrary extension.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary x∈Space and t>0, with j,k as declared and put p=(x,t), w(y,r)=ubar(y,r)_k, T=(0,1), Xdir=(basis(j),0). F001 and continuous linear scalar projection give w C∞ on the open set U. Apply M006 over ℝ, with domain Space×ℝ, scalar codomain and both smoothness orders ∞: ∞+1=∞ supplies the order inequality, so Dw is C∞ on U. The derivative of the affine time injection r↦(x,r) sends h to (0,h); the derivative of y↦(y,t) sends h to (h,0). The ordinary chain rule identifies V(x,t)_k=Dw(p)T and Psp(j,x,t)_k=Dw(p)Xdir, first as HasDerivAt or HasFDerivAt assertions, then as equalities by uniqueness. These identities hold on all U, not just at p. Evaluation at a fixed direction is continuous linear, so the identities and smoothness of Dw show that V and every Psp(j) are C∞ on U, componentwise and hence as finite vector-valued maps. In particular the actual time derivative of each coordinate of ubar is V. Record F002 with these first-derivative and smoothness facts.

produces.statement: V and Psp(j0) are C∞ on U for every j0∈Fin n. For every x0∈Space,t1>0,k0∈Fin m, HasDerivAt (r↦ubar(x0,r)_k0) V(x0,t1)_k0 t1; the spatial derivative in direction basis(j0) is Psp(j0,x0,t1)_k0. At the chosen p, V(x,t)_k=Dw(p)T and Psp(j,x,t)_k=Dw(p)Xdir.

argument.text: Put Hess(v,w0)=D(Dw)(p)(v)(w0). Apply M006 again, this time to the C∞ map Dw with its continuous-linear-map codomain, and iterate for higher derivatives as needed; U is open and the ∞ order inequality remains valid. Differentiate the fixed evaluations from S002 by the chain rule. This gives ∂_t Psp(j,x,t)_k=Hess(T,Xdir), ∂_j V(x,t)_k=Hess(Xdir,T), A(x,t)_k=Hess(T,T), and Ssp(j,x,t)_k=Hess(Xdir,Xdir). F001 gives C² regularity of w at p because p∈U. Apply M005 over ℝ at order 2, where minSmoothness(ℝ,2)=2, to get Hess(T,Xdir)=Hess(Xdir,T). By the definition of W the common value is W(j,x,t)_k. The same derivative closure and fixed evaluations show A,Ssp(j),W(j) C∞ on U; this holds at every positive point and for every coordinate. Record F003: the full second-derivative regularity and the actual time derivative identities for V and Psp.

produces.statement: A, Ssp(j0), W(j0) are C∞ on U for every j0∈Fin n. For all x0∈Space,t1>0,k0∈Fin m,j0∈Fin n, HasDerivAt (r↦V(x0,r)_k0) A(x0,t1)_k0 t1 and HasDerivAt (r↦Psp(j0,x0,r)_k0) W(j0,x0,t1)_k0 t1. The spatial j0 derivative of V_k0 is W(j0)_k0 and the spatial j0 derivative of Psp(j0)_k0 is Ssp(j0)_k0.

argument.text: Apply M004 over ℝ to the time function V(x,·)_k multiplied by itself, using F003, to obtain derivative 2 V(x,t)_k A(x,t)_k for its square. Apply M004 also to Psp(j,x,·)_k multiplied by itself, using its time derivative W(j,x,t)_k from F003, to obtain 2 Psp(j,x,t)_k W(j,x,t)_k. The coordinate k and spatial index j are arbitrary; finite-sum differentiation therefore gives HasDerivAt (r↦e(x,r)) [2∑_k V(x,t)_k A(x,t)_k+2∑_j∑_k Psp(j,x,t)_k W(j,x,t)_k] t. Finite distributivity identifies the bracket with d(x,t). Smooth finite products and sums of F002 and F003 also show e and d are C∞ on U. Record F004: the displayed HasDerivAt identity with derivative d, and C∞ regularity of e,d.

The identified Laplacian is exactly L=∑_j Ssp(j), and the identified density and measure give the original total energy expression E without any change of coefficient. This proves the full exported representation and smooth-calculus assertion.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary t0>0. The inequalities 0<t0/2<3t0/2 allow H006 to choose compact C such that u=q off C throughout J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Put I=(t0/2,3t0/2). All times of J are positive, so the definition of ubar gives the same equality for ubar. In particular t0∈I. Record F001: C is compact and ubar=q on Cᶜ×J.

argument.text: A compact subset C of the Hausdorff finite-dimensional space is closed. Thus O=Cᶜ×I is open. At each arbitrary p∈O the equality in F001 holds on a whole neighborhood: ubar is locally the constant q. Apply M007 to ubar and that constant on this neighborhood. The constant has zero derivative (its increments are zero), so D ubar(p)=0. This holds at every point of O. Reapply M007 to this derivative map and the zero map at every point of O; its derivative is again zero. Induction on the positive derivative order now gives every such derivative zero on O. The first-order case is established. For the step fix an arbitrary positive natural order ell and temporarily assume L1: the order-ell derivative map is zero throughout O. Then each point has a neighborhood on which that map is the constant zero, so M007 makes its next derivative zero there. Discharge L1 to obtain the induction step; natural induction gives all positive orders. Restricting the locally constant map and its derivative maps along the affine time and spatial sections, the ordinary chain rule identifies V,A,Psp,Ssp,W with the corresponding directional evaluations of the first two derivatives; their component section derivatives are the actual ones asserted in N001. Consequently V=A=Psp(j)=Ssp(j)=W(j)=0 on O for all j, and the formulas for e,d make both zero there. Record F002 with this universal vanishing conclusion.

produces.statement: Every positive-order spacetime derivative of ubar vanishes on O=Cᶜ×I. In particular V,A,Psp(j1),Ssp(j1),W(j1),e,d vanish there for every j1∈Fin n.

argument.text: Fix arbitrary r∈I and take the family of sections specified in the local declaration. By N001 each component section is continuous on the whole spatial space; e,d are continuous as well. Finite products, sums and dot products preserve continuity. F002 makes each of these sections zero off C. For an arbitrary section h in this family, support h⊆C. Since C is closed, its closure tsupport h is also contained in C; tsupport h is closed and hence a compact closed subset of the compact C. Apply M001 with domain Space, codomain ℝ and measure dx to h. This is a Borel real normed coordinate space; its Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets. For example a compact set is contained in some finite coordinate box, whose product Lebesgue measure is finite, and monotonicity bounds the compact set's measure. Therefore the source gives dx-integrability of every such h. Record F003: all the stated sections at r have compact topological support contained in C and are integrable.

produces.statement: At the arbitrary r∈I, the arbitrary h∈family is continuous with tsupport h⊆C, has compact topological support, and is dx-integrable.

In particular every positive time has an integrable energy density. No vanishing assertion at the endpoints of J has been used.

Set Kprod=C×Ktime. Compactness of C from N002 and compactness of the closed bounded real interval Ktime show that Kprod is compact. It lies in U. argument.text: Choose B0 from F001 and put B=max(B0,0), bnd=B·1_C. The compact subset C of the Hausdorff coordinate space is closed and hence Borel measurable. Its Lebesgue measure is finite: compactness bounds it in a finite coordinate box and dx of that box is the finite product of its side lengths. The real number B has finite extended norm. M009, with scalar value B and set C, gives IntegrableOn (constant B) C dx. M010, using measurability of C, turns this into Integrable bnd dx. Thus record F002: bnd is an integrable nonnegative bound, and |d(x,r)|≤B on C×Ktime.

argument.text: For each spatial x and every r∈stime, if x∈C the compact bound in F002 gives |d(x,r)|≤B=bnd(x); if x∉C, N002 gives d(x,r)=0 and bnd(x)=0. Consequently the entire predicate ∀ r∈stime, |d(x,r)|≤bnd(x) holds for every x, and hence for dx-almost every x with a single, empty exceptional set. Separately N001 gives HasDerivAt (s↦e(x,s)) d(x,r) r for every x and every r∈stime, because all these times are positive. Thus this universal-in-r predicate also holds for dx-almost every x. N001 gives continuity of e(·,r) for r∈stime and of d(·,t0); continuous real functions on the Borel coordinate space are strongly measurable and hence ae strongly measurable. This supplies eventual measurability of e because stime is a neighborhood. N002 gives integrability of e(·,t0). Record F003 with these premises, preserving the ae-first order in both quantified hypotheses.

For a vector in any such coordinate space, its maximum coordinate norm is at most its Euclidean norm, and its Euclidean norm is at most the square root of the number of coordinates times its maximum coordinate norm. Thus the coordinate identity and its inverse are continuous linear maps; they preserve Fréchet differentiability and all C∞ orders by the chain rule. The coordinates are the original standard ones, so dot and normSq are exactly the original dot product and squared Euclidean norm, not the product norm squared. Lebesgue measure in these standard coordinates is by definition the product of the usual real coordinate Lebesgue measures, giving dx with no Jacobian or rescaling. Restricting ubar to U recovers u, and conversely extension by q gives the total ubar. At a point of U a neighborhood stays in U, so all derivatives there are local and independent of the extension at nonpositive times. H002 therefore gives C∞ regularity of ubar on U. The derivative definitions, finite coordinate sums and the measure identification give the asserted meanings of V,A,Psp,Ssp,L,e,E once their actual derivative identities are checked below. Record F001: this coordinate representation, measure and norm identification is faithful, and ubar is C∞ on U.

Fix arbitrary x∈Space and t>0, with j,k as declared and put p=(x,t), w(y,r)=ubar(y,r)_k, T=(0,1), Xdir=(basis(j),0). F001 and continuous linear scalar projection give w C∞ on the open set U. Apply M006 over ℝ, with domain Space×ℝ, scalar codomain and both smoothness orders ∞: ∞+1=∞ supplies the order inequality, so Dw is C∞ on U. The derivative of the affine time injection r↦(x,r) sends h to (0,h); the derivative of y↦(y,t) sends h to (h,0). The ordinary chain rule identifies V(x,t)_k=Dw(p)T and Psp(j,x,t)_k=Dw(p)Xdir, first as HasDerivAt or HasFDerivAt assertions, then as equalities by uniqueness. These identities hold on all U, not just at p. Evaluation at a fixed direction is continuous linear, so the identities and smoothness of Dw show that V and every Psp(j) are C∞ on U, componentwise and hence as finite vector-valued maps. In particular the actual time derivative of each coordinate of ubar is V. Record F002 with these first-derivative and smoothness facts.

Put Hess(v,w0)=D(Dw)(p)(v)(w0). Apply M006 again, this time to the C∞ map Dw with its continuous-linear-map codomain, and iterate for higher derivatives as needed; U is open and the ∞ order inequality remains valid. Differentiate the fixed evaluations from S002 by the chain rule. This gives ∂_t Psp(j,x,t)_k=Hess(T,Xdir), ∂_j V(x,t)_k=Hess(Xdir,T), A(x,t)_k=Hess(T,T), and Ssp(j,x,t)_k=Hess(Xdir,Xdir). F001 gives C² regularity of w at p because p∈U. Apply M005 over ℝ at order 2, where minSmoothness(ℝ,2)=2, to get Hess(T,Xdir)=Hess(Xdir,T). By the definition of W the common value is W(j,x,t)_k. The same derivative closure and fixed evaluations show A,Ssp(j),W(j) C∞ on U; this holds at every positive point and for every coordinate. Record F003: the full second-derivative regularity and the actual time derivative identities for V and Psp.

Apply M004 over ℝ to the time function V(x,·)_k multiplied by itself, using F003, to obtain derivative 2 V(x,t)_k A(x,t)_k for its square. Apply M004 also to Psp(j,x,·)_k multiplied by itself, using its time derivative W(j,x,t)_k from F003, to obtain 2 Psp(j,x,t)_k W(j,x,t)_k. The coordinate k and spatial index j are arbitrary; finite-sum differentiation therefore gives HasDerivAt (r↦e(x,r)) [2∑_k V(x,t)_k A(x,t)_k+2∑_j∑_k Psp(j,x,t)_k W(j,x,t)_k] t. Finite distributivity identifies the bracket with d(x,t). Smooth finite products and sums of F002 and F003 also show e and d are C∞ on U. Record F004: the displayed HasDerivAt identity with derivative d, and C∞ regularity of e,d.

The spatial derivative identities for ubar, Psp and V are their definitions; F002 and F003 verify that they are genuine derivatives at positive times. Combining F001–F004 proves all regularity, mixed-derivative and energy-derivative clauses. Since x,t,j,k were arbitrary, close their quantifiers. The identified Laplacian is exactly L=∑_j Ssp(j), and the identified density and measure give the original total energy expression E without any change of coefficient. This proves the full exported representation and smooth-calculus assertion.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. The inequalities 0<t0/2<3t0/2 allow H006 to choose compact C such that u=q off C throughout J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Put I=(t0/2,3t0/2). All times of J are positive, so the definition of ubar gives the same equality for ubar. In particular t0∈I. Record F001: C is compact and ubar=q on Cᶜ×J.

A compact subset C of the Hausdorff finite-dimensional space is closed. Thus O=Cᶜ×I is open. At each arbitrary p∈O the equality in F001 holds on a whole neighborhood: ubar is locally the constant q. Apply M007 to ubar and that constant on this neighborhood. The constant has zero derivative (its increments are zero), so D ubar(p)=0. This holds at every point of O. Reapply M007 to this derivative map and the zero map at every point of O; its derivative is again zero. Induction on the positive derivative order now gives every such derivative zero on O. The first-order case is established. For the step fix an arbitrary positive natural order ell and temporarily assume L1: the order-ell derivative map is zero throughout O. Then each point has a neighborhood on which that map is the constant zero, so M007 makes its next derivative zero there. Discharge L1 to obtain the induction step; natural induction gives all positive orders. Restricting the locally constant map and its derivative maps along the affine time and spatial sections, the ordinary chain rule identifies V,A,Psp,Ssp,W with the corresponding directional evaluations of the first two derivatives; their component section derivatives are the actual ones asserted in N001. Consequently V=A=Psp(j)=Ssp(j)=W(j)=0 on O for all j, and the formulas for e,d make both zero there. Record F002 with this universal vanishing conclusion.

Fix arbitrary r∈I and take the family of sections specified in the local declaration. By N001 each component section is continuous on the whole spatial space; e,d are continuous as well. Finite products, sums and dot products preserve continuity. F002 makes each of these sections zero off C. For an arbitrary section h in this family, support h⊆C. Since C is closed, its closure tsupport h is also contained in C; tsupport h is closed and hence a compact closed subset of the compact C. Apply M001 with domain Space, codomain ℝ and measure dx to h. This is a Borel real normed coordinate space; its Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets. For example a compact set is contained in some finite coordinate box, whose product Lebesgue measure is finite, and monotonicity bounds the compact set's measure. Therefore the source gives dx-integrability of every such h. Record F003: all the stated sections at r have compact topological support contained in C and are integrable.

The conclusions hold for every r∈I and every stated component, product, dot product and finite linear combination. Since t0∈I, this proves integrability of e(·,t0). The existence and vanishing conclusions depend only on the chosen slab and thus give the full exported existential support statement after closing the choice of C and the arbitrary t0. In particular every positive time has an integrable energy density. No vanishing assertion at the endpoints of J has been used.

Fix t0>0 and choose C from N002 with its full conclusions. Put I=(t0/2,3t0/2), eta=t0/4>0, Ktime=[t0−eta,t0+eta], stime=(t0−eta,t0+eta). Explicitly t0−eta=3t0/4>t0/2 and t0+eta=5t0/4<3t0/2. Thus Ktime⊂I⊂(0,∞), and stime is an open neighborhood of t0. N002 supplies vanishing of d off C for all these times, and integrability and continuity of the spatial sections e,d throughout I.

Set Kprod=C×Ktime. Compactness of C from N002 and compactness of the closed bounded real interval Ktime show that Kprod is compact. It lies in U. N001 makes d continuous on U, so its restriction is continuous on Kprod. Apply M008 to d on Kprod to obtain a real bound for |d|. Record F001: there exists a real bound on Kprod. This existence assertion is valid also for empty C.

Choose B0 from F001 and put B=max(B0,0), bnd=B·1_C. The compact subset C of the Hausdorff coordinate space is closed and hence Borel measurable. Its Lebesgue measure is finite: compactness bounds it in a finite coordinate box and dx of that box is the finite product of its side lengths. The real number B has finite extended norm. M009, with scalar value B and set C, gives IntegrableOn (constant B) C dx. M010, using measurability of C, turns this into Integrable bnd dx. Thus record F002: bnd is an integrable nonnegative bound, and |d(x,r)|≤B on C×Ktime.

For each spatial x and every r∈stime, if x∈C the compact bound in F002 gives |d(x,r)|≤B=bnd(x); if x∉C, N002 gives d(x,r)=0 and bnd(x)=0. Consequently the entire predicate ∀ r∈stime, |d(x,r)|≤bnd(x) holds for every x, and hence for dx-almost every x with a single, empty exceptional set. Separately N001 gives HasDerivAt (s↦e(x,s)) d(x,r) r for every x and every r∈stime, because all these times are positive. Thus this universal-in-r predicate also holds for dx-almost every x. N001 gives continuity of e(·,r) for r∈stime and of d(·,t0); continuous real functions on the Borel coordinate space are strongly measurable and hence ae strongly measurable. This supplies eventual measurability of e because stime is a neighborhood. N002 gives integrability of e(·,t0). Record F003 with these premises, preserving the ae-first order in both quantified hypotheses.

Apply M002 with α=Space, μ=dx, real parameter and codomain, F(r,x)=e(x,r), F'(r,x)=d(x,r), basepoint t0, neighborhood stime and bound bnd. F003 gives its neighborhood, eventual measurability, base integrability, derivative-section measurability, ae-first bound and ae-first derivative premises. F002 gives integrability of the bound. M002 concludes Integrable d(·,t0) and HasDerivAt (r↦∫ e(x,r) dx) (∫ d(x,t0) dx) t0. By the definition of E this is the desired derivative statement for the actual energy integral. N002 ensures that the integrals e defining E are finite at all positive times, so this is differentiability of the requested finite function.

The bound, compact set and time neighborhood were allowed to depend on the arbitrary t0>0. Eliminate their local choices and close the quantifier on t0 in F004. This proves the exported derivative statement; no bound over the whole half-space or assertion at zero has been added.

Fix arbitrary x and t>0. H004 and the coordinate identification in N001 give ∑_k ubar(x,r)_k²=1 for every r>0, hence on a neighborhood of t. For arbitrary k apply M004 over ℝ to ubar(x,·)_k multiplied by itself; N001 supplies its actual derivative V(x,t)_k. The square has derivative 2 ubar(x,t)_k V(x,t)_k. Differentiating the finite sum gives derivative 2 dot(ubar(x,t),V(x,t)). Since the sum agrees locally with the constant 1, its derivative is zero by locality and uniqueness of derivatives. Division by 2 yields dot(ubar,V)=0; commutativity of real multiplication yields dot(V,ubar)=0. Record F001: these two tangency identities at (x,t).

At this point take just the scalar witness a0 from H005. N001 identifies the original u_tt and Δ_xu with A and L, and u with ubar, so A(x,t)−L(x,t)=a0 ubar(x,t). By finite distributivity of dot and F001, dot(V,A−L)=dot(V,a0 ubar)=a0 dot(V,ubar)=0. Record F002: the required normality cancellation at (x,t). This uses no function selecting scalar witnesses and no derivative of the witness.

Both identities are independent of the chosen scalar's identity. Eliminate that existential choice and universally quantify the arbitrary x and positive t. F001 and F002 prove the exported tangency and cancellation identities. The optional explicit scalar formula and twice-differentiated unit constraint from the original proof are not needed by this authorized route.

Fix arbitrary t0>0,j∈Fin n,k∈Fin m. On the entire spatial space set f(x)=V(x,t0)_k, g(x)=Psp(j,x,t0)_k and v=basis(j). N001 gives their C∞ regularity as spatial sections: the affine inclusion x↦(x,t0) stays in U and smoothness is local at each point. Thus f and g are differentiable everywhere, in particular on the respective topological supports of g and f. The actual directional derivatives from N001 are Df(x)v=W(j,x,t0)_k and Dg(x)v=Ssp(j,x,t0)_k. By N002 at time t0, all three products (Df v)g, f(Dg v) and fg are continuous with compact support and integrable: they are W(j)_k Psp(j)_k, V_k Ssp(j)_k and V_k Psp(j)_k. Record F001 with these derivative and applicability facts.

Apply M003 on the finite-dimensional real space Space with its Borel structure, canonical Lebesgue additive Haar measure dx, scalar field ℝ, functions f,g and direction v. The hypotheses are F001. The conclusion is exactly ∫ V(x,t0)_k Ssp(j,x,t0)_k dx = −∫ W(j,x,t0)_k Psp(j,x,t0)_k dx. Record this scalar identity as F002.

Because k was arbitrary, F002 holds for every k∈Fin m. Sum these finitely many identities. N002 supplies integrability of each summand, so finite-sum linearity commutes integral and sum. Expanding dot gives ∫ dot(V,Ssp(j)) = −∫ dot(W(j),Psp(j)). Real multiplication commutes in each coordinate, hence dot(W(j),Psp(j))=dot(Psp(j),W(j)). Negating and rearranging gives ∫ dot(Psp(j),W(j)) = −∫ dot(V,Ssp(j)). Both integrands are integrable by N002, as are all the auxiliary products already checked. Record F003: the integration-by-parts identity at t0,j, including those integrability assertions.
Close the arbitrary j and positive t0 in F003. This is precisely the exported assertion, with the whole-space integration-by-parts identity required for the final energy calculation.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. N002 gives integrability of e(·,t0), d(·,t0), each component product V_k A_k, Psp(j)_k W(j)_k and V_k Ssp(j)_k, and their dot products and finite linear combinations. Thus every integral in the following finite calculation is well-defined and finite. N003 gives HasDerivAt E (∫ d(x,t0) dx) t0. Record F001 with this derivative statement and the integrability facts just listed.

Use F001 to distribute finite sums and real scalar factors through integrals, the definition of d, N005 for each j, and L=∑_j Ssp(j). All integrands here are evaluated at (x,t0):
∫ d = 2∫ dot(V,A) + 2∑_j ∫ dot(Psp(j),W(j))
     = 2∫ dot(V,A) − 2∑_j ∫ dot(V,Ssp(j))
     = 2∫ dot(V,A−∑_j Ssp(j))
     = 2∫ dot(V,A−L) = 0.
The penultimate algebra uses finite distributivity of dot and the integral's linearity for the integrable terms in F001. The last equality follows from the pointwise cancellation N004 at every x and positive t0, followed by the integral of the zero function. Hence the derivative value in F001 is zero. Record F002: HasDerivAt E 0 t0.

HasDerivAt E 0 t0 in F002 implies differentiability at t0 and E'(t0)=0 by the definition and uniqueness of the derivative. N002 already gives integrability of e(·,t0), so E(t0) is the actual finite energy, not a value assigned by the total integral convention. N001 identifies every derivative, Euclidean square, Frobenius finite sum and the measure with the original target. Thus the original density has coefficient 1 on |u_t|² and on each spatial derivative square, and the original E is differentiable with derivative zero at every positive time. Close the arbitrary t0 to obtain the full target conclusion, including integrability. No assertion at time zero is made.

import Mathlib
open scoped Topology ContDiff
open MeasureTheory Filter
namespace WaveMapEnergy
abbrev Space (n : ℕ) := Fin n → ℝ
abbrev Value (m : ℕ) := Fin m → ℝ
def dot {m : ℕ} (v w : Value m) : ℝ := ∑ k, v k * w k
def normSq {m : ℕ} (v : Value m) : ℝ := dot v v
noncomputable def velocity {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => deriv (fun r => u (x, r) k) t
noncomputable def acceleration {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => deriv (fun r => velocity u x r k) t
noncomputable def spatial {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => fderiv ℝ (fun y => u (y, t) k) x (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def spatialSecond {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => fderiv ℝ (fun y => spatial u j y t k) x (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def laplacian {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m := ∑ j, spatialSecond u j x t
noncomputable def density {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  normSq (velocity u x t) + ∑ j, normSq (spatial u j x t)
noncomputable def energy {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∫ x, density u x t
def Smooth {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ u {p | 0 < p.2}
def UnitValued {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ∀ x t, 0 < t → normSq (u (x, t)) = 1
def Normal {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ∀ x t, 0 < t → ∃ a : ℝ, acceleration u x t - laplacian u x t = a • u (x, t)
def CompactPerturbation {n m : ℕ} (u : Space n × ℝ → Value m) (q : Value m) : Prop :=
  ∀ s t : ℝ, 0 < s → s < t → ∃ C : Set (Space n), IsCompact C ∧
    ∀ x r, x ∉ C → r ∈ Set.Icc s t → u (x, r) = q
end WaveMapEnergy

namespace WaveMapEnergy
noncomputable def ubar {n m : ℕ}
    (u : Space n × Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ) → Value m) (q : Value m)
    (p : Space n × ℝ) : Value m :=
  if h : 0 < p.2 then u (p.1, ⟨p.2, h⟩) else q
noncomputable def mixed {n m : ℕ} (v : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : Value m :=
  fun k => fderiv ℝ (fun y => velocity v y t k) x (Pi.single j 1)
noncomputable def densityRate {n m : ℕ} (v : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (x : Space n) (t : ℝ) : ℝ :=
  2 * dot (velocity v x t) (acceleration v x t) +
    2 * ∑ j, dot (spatial v j x t) (mixed v j x t)
def FirstCalculus {n m : ℕ} (v : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  Smooth v ∧
  ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (fun p : Space n × ℝ => velocity v p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2} ∧
  (∀ j : Fin n, ContDiffOn ℝ ∞
    (fun p : Space n × ℝ => spatial v j p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2}) ∧
  (∀ (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ k : Fin m,
    HasDerivAt (fun r => v (x,r) k) (velocity v x t k) t) ∧
  (∀ (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ k : Fin m,
    HasFDerivAt (fun y => v (y,t) k) (fderiv ℝ (fun y => v (y,t) k) x) x)
def SecondCalculus {n m : ℕ} (v : Space n × ℝ → Value m) : Prop :=
  ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (fun p : Space n × ℝ => acceleration v p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2} ∧
  (∀ j : Fin n, ContDiffOn ℝ ∞
    (fun p : Space n × ℝ => spatialSecond v j p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2}) ∧
  (∀ j : Fin n, ContDiffOn ℝ ∞
    (fun p : Space n × ℝ => mixed v j p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2}) ∧
  (∀ (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ k : Fin m,
    HasDerivAt (fun r => velocity v x r k) (acceleration v x t k) t) ∧
  (∀ (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ k : Fin m,
    HasDerivAt (fun r => spatial v j x r k) (mixed v j x t k) t) ∧
  (∀ (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ k : Fin m,
    HasFDerivAt (fun y => velocity v y t k)
      (fderiv ℝ (fun y => velocity v y t k) x) x ∧
    HasFDerivAt (fun y => spatial v j y t k)
      (fderiv ℝ (fun y => spatial v j y t k) x) x)
noncomputable def sections {n m : ℕ} (v : Space n × ℝ → Value m)
    (t : ℝ) : Set (Space n → ℝ) :=
  {h | h = (fun x => density v x t) ∨ h = (fun x => densityRate v x t) ∨
    (∃ k : Fin m, h = (fun x => velocity v x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => acceleration v x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => velocity v x t k * acceleration v x t k)) ∨
    (∃ (j : Fin n) (k : Fin m),
      h = (fun x => spatial v j x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => spatialSecond v j x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => mixed v j x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => spatial v j x t k * mixed v j x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => velocity v x t k * spatialSecond v j x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => velocity v x t k * spatial v j x t k) ∨
      h = (fun x => mixed v j x t k * spatial v j x t k)) ∨
    h = (fun x => dot (velocity v x t) (acceleration v x t)) ∨
    (∃ j : Fin n,
      h = (fun x => dot (spatial v j x t) (mixed v j x t)) ∨
      h = (fun x => dot (velocity v x t) (spatialSecond v j x t)) ∨
      h = (fun x => dot (velocity v x t) (spatial v j x t)) ∨
      h = (fun x => dot (mixed v j x t) (spatial v j x t)))}
def SupportedSection {n : ℕ} (C : Set (Space n)) (h : Space n → ℝ) : Prop :=
  Continuous h ∧ tsupport h ⊆ C ∧ HasCompactSupport h ∧ Integrable h
def SlabVanishing {n m : ℕ} (v : Space n × ℝ → Value m) (q : Value m)
    (t₀ : ℝ) (C : Set (Space n)) : Prop :=
  IsCompact C ∧
  (∀ x r, x ∉ C → r ∈ Set.Icc (t₀/2) (3*t₀/2) → v (x,r) = q) ∧
  (∀ (ell : ℕ), 0 < ell → ∀ x r,
    x ∉ C → r ∈ Set.Ioo (t₀/2) (3*t₀/2) → iteratedFDeriv ℝ ell v (x,r) = 0) ∧
  (∀ x r, x ∉ C → r ∈ Set.Ioo (t₀/2) (3*t₀/2) →
    velocity v x r = 0 ∧ acceleration v x r = 0 ∧
    (∀ j, spatial v j x r = 0 ∧ spatialSecond v j x r = 0 ∧ mixed v j x r = 0) ∧
    density v x r = 0 ∧ densityRate v x r = 0)
end WaveMapEnergy
open WaveMapEnergy

value.type: Space n × Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ) → Value m

value.statement: n≥1 and m≥1.
u is jointly C∞ on ℝⁿ×(0,∞).
q∈ℝᵐ satisfies |q|=1 for the Euclidean norm.
For every x∈ℝⁿ and t>0, |u(x,t)|=1 for the Euclidean norm.
For every x∈ℝⁿ and t>0 there exists a real scalar a such that u_tt(x,t)−Δ_x u(x,t)=a u(x,t), with Δ_x u=∑_{j=1}^n ∂_{x_jx_j}u componentwise. No regularity or global choice of the scalar is assumed.
For every pair of real numbers 0<s<t<∞ there exists a compact C⊆ℝⁿ such that u(x,r)=q for every x∉C and every r∈[s,t].

P.explanation: Parameters n,m are natural dimensions with H001 enforcing n,m≥1, equivalent to the specified positive integer dimensions. The parameter u has exactly the original positive-time domain in fixed standard coordinates; q is the fixed vector. H002 requires smoothness only on the positive open half-space of its canonical extension ubar, equivalent in both directions to joint smoothness of the original map by restriction and local agreement. H003 and H004 use normSq=∑k v_k²=1, equivalent over ℝ to Euclidean norm 1 since that norm is nonnegative. H005 retains ∀x,t>0 ∃a:ℝ with A−L=a•ubar and imposes no regularity or global choice of a. H006 keeps ∀0<s<t ∃compact C ∀x∉C ∀r∈[s,t], ubar=q, so support remains locally uniform in time. Restricting ubar recovers u and extending u by q recovers ubar; all derivatives at positive times are local and unchanged. Standard coordinate identities preserve the finite-dimensional topology and Fréchet derivatives in both directions, while normSq and finite spatial sums are exactly the Euclidean and Frobenius squares and volume is exactly product Lebesgue measure. The conclusion explicitly quantifies every real t>0 and proves integrability of the coefficient-1 density, DifferentiableAt of its actual energy integral, and deriv=0. Thus the complete target and all hypotheses correspond in both directions; there is no additional assertion at zero, stronger support requirement, or assumption on the scalar witness.

value.statement: For every real t>0, e(·,t) is Lebesgue integrable on ℝⁿ, the finite energy E is differentiable at t, and E'(t)=0. Here e=|u_t|²+∑_{j=1}^n|∂_{x_j}u|² and E(t)=∫_{ℝⁿ}e(x,t) dx with Euclidean norms and Lebesgue measure; there is no assertion at time zero.
value.type: ∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → Integrable (fun x => density (ubar u q) x t) ∧ DifferentiableAt ℝ (energy (ubar u q)) t ∧ deriv (energy (ubar u q)) t = 0

steps.statement: FirstCalculus (ubar u q)
steps.explanation: Use the standard coordinate identity and affine time/spatial injections on the open positive half-space. Scalar coordinate projection and open-set derivative closure give smooth velocity and spatial fields and their actual first derivatives. The prepared product norm is used only for topology/calculus; dot and normSq retain the Euclidean metric. ContDiff exponents live in WithTop ℕ∞: the scoped ∞ is the embedded infinite natural, not the analytic top ω.

steps.statement: SecondCalculus (ubar u q)
steps.explanation: Differentiate the first-derivative evaluations along the same fixed injections. Apply second Fréchet derivative symmetry over ℝ to interchange the spatial and time directions. The pinned minSmoothness ℝ 2 equals 2 because ℝ is IsRCLikeNormedField; use the two-smoothness consequence of FirstCalculus. Iterate open-set derivative closure for smoothness of the second-order fields. Supply named field/order/set arguments when inference needs them.

steps.statement:
FirstCalculus (ubar u q) ∧ SecondCalculus (ubar u q) ∧
ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (fun p : Space n × ℝ => density (ubar u q) p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2} ∧
ContDiffOn ℝ ∞ (fun p : Space n × ℝ => densityRate (ubar u q) p.1 p.2) {p | 0 < p.2} ∧
(∀ (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → HasDerivAt (fun r => density (ubar u q) x r) (densityRate (ubar u q) x t) t) ∧
(∀ (j : Fin n) (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), 0 < t → ∀ k : Fin m,
 fderiv ℝ (fun y => (ubar u q) (y,t) k) x (Pi.single j 1) = spatial (ubar u q) j x t k ∧
 fderiv ℝ (fun y => velocity (ubar u q) y t k) x (Pi.single j 1) = mixed (ubar u q) j x t k ∧
 fderiv ℝ (fun y => spatial (ubar u q) j y t k) x (Pi.single j 1) = spatialSecond (ubar u q) j x t k) ∧
(∀ (x : Space n) (t : Set.Ioi (0 : ℝ)), (ubar u q) (x,t) = u (x,t)) ∧
(∀ (x : Space n) (t : ℝ), t ≤ 0 → (ubar u q) (x,t) = q)
steps.explanation: Export all of N001. Product differentiation of each squared coordinate and finite sums gives densityRate, with coefficient 2 in the derivative and coefficient 1 in density. Smoothness follows from finite products and sums. The three spatial equalities unfold the prepared definitions. Restriction/extension identities make the domain correspondence explicit; the Laplacian and energy are definitionally the specified finite sum and volume integral. No smoothness at zero is asserted.

steps.statement: ∀ t₀ : ℝ, 0 < t₀ → ∃ C : Set (Space n), SlabVanishing (ubar u q) q t₀ C
steps.explanation: Choose the compact set on [t₀/2,3t₀/2] from H006. Its complement times the open slab is open and ubar is locally constant there. Locality of the Fréchet derivative, iterated by induction, proves vanishing of every positive-order iteratedFDeriv; ell is a natural derivative order, with ell>0 excluding order zero. Restrict to the time/spatial sections to obtain all named zero fields and then the zero densities.

steps.statement:
(∀ t₀ : ℝ, 0 < t₀ → ∃ C : Set (Space n),
 SlabVanishing (ubar u q) q t₀ C ∧
 ∀ r ∈ Set.Ioo (t₀/2) (3*t₀/2),
 ∀ h ∈ Submodule.span ℝ (sections (ubar u q) r), SupportedSection C h) ∧
(∀ t : ℝ, 0 < t → Integrable (fun x => density (ubar u q) x t))
steps.explanation: Export N002 with the same compact witness. sections lists exactly the source component sections, five scalar product families, energy density and its rate, and the five dot-product families. Submodule.span over ℝ means all finite real linear combinations, including the generators. Each section is continuous and zero off the closed compact C, so its topological support is contained in C, compact, and its integral is finite. Use direct library compact-support integrability, then closure under finite linear combinations. Since t₀ lies inside its slab, conclude integrability at every positive time.

Compactness gives measurability and finite volume, hence integrability of b. Outside C the rate vanishes. value.text: H001 fixes positive finite dimensions. Use the fixed standard coordinates on both original Euclidean spaces. For a vector in any such coordinate space, its maximum coordinate norm is at most its Euclidean norm, and its Euclidean norm is at most the square root of the number of coordinates times its maximum coordinate norm. Thus the coordinate identity and its inverse are continuous linear maps; they preserve Fréchet differentiability and all C∞ orders by the chain rule. The coordinates are the original standard ones, so dot and normSq are exactly the original dot product and squared Euclidean norm, not the product norm squared. Lebesgue measure in these standard coordinates is by definition the product of the usual real coordinate Lebesgue measures, giving dx with no Jacobian or rescaling. Restricting ubar to U recovers u, and conversely extension by q gives the total ubar. At a point of U a neighborhood stays in U, so all derivatives there are local and independent of the extension at nonpositive times. H002 therefore gives C∞ regularity of ubar on U. The derivative definitions, finite coordinate sums and the measure identification give the asserted meanings of V,A,Psp,Ssp,L,e,E once their actual derivative identities are checked below. Record F001: this coordinate representation, measure and norm identification is faithful, and ubar is C∞ on U.

Fix arbitrary x∈Space and t>0, with j,k as declared and put p=(x,t), w(y,r)=ubar(y,r)_k, T=(0,1), Xdir=(basis(j),0). F001 and continuous linear scalar projection give w C∞ on the open set U. Apply M006 over ℝ, with domain Space×ℝ, scalar codomain and both smoothness orders ∞: ∞+1=∞ supplies the order inequality, so Dw is C∞ on U. The derivative of the affine time injection r↦(x,r) sends h to (0,h); the derivative of y↦(y,t) sends h to (h,0). The ordinary chain rule identifies V(x,t)_k=Dw(p)T and Psp(j,x,t)_k=Dw(p)Xdir, first as HasDerivAt or HasFDerivAt assertions, then as equalities by uniqueness. These identities hold on all U, not just at p. Evaluation at a fixed direction is continuous linear, so the identities and smoothness of Dw show that V and every Psp(j) are C∞ on U, componentwise and hence as finite vector-valued maps. In particular the actual time derivative of each coordinate of ubar is V. Record F002 with these first-derivative and smoothness facts.

Put Hess(v,w0)=D(Dw)(p)(v)(w0). Apply M006 again, this time to the C∞ map Dw with its continuous-linear-map codomain, and iterate for higher derivatives as needed; U is open and the ∞ order inequality remains valid. Differentiate the fixed evaluations from S002 by the chain rule. This gives ∂_t Psp(j,x,t)_k=Hess(T,Xdir), ∂_j V(x,t)_k=Hess(Xdir,T), A(x,t)_k=Hess(T,T), and Ssp(j,x,t)_k=Hess(Xdir,Xdir). F001 gives C² regularity of w at p because p∈U. Apply M005 over ℝ at order 2, where minSmoothness(ℝ,2)=2, to get Hess(T,Xdir)=Hess(Xdir,T). By the definition of W the common value is W(j,x,t)_k. The same derivative closure and fixed evaluations show A,Ssp(j),W(j) C∞ on U; this holds at every positive point and for every coordinate. Record F003: the full second-derivative regularity and the actual time derivative identities for V and Psp.

Apply M004 over ℝ to the time function V(x,·)_k multiplied by itself, using F003, to obtain derivative 2 V(x,t)_k A(x,t)_k for its square. Apply M004 also to Psp(j,x,·)_k multiplied by itself, using its time derivative W(j,x,t)_k from F003, to obtain 2 Psp(j,x,t)_k W(j,x,t)_k. The coordinate k and spatial index j are arbitrary; finite-sum differentiation therefore gives HasDerivAt (r↦e(x,r)) [2∑_k V(x,t)_k A(x,t)_k+2∑_j∑_k Psp(j,x,t)_k W(j,x,t)_k] t. Finite distributivity identifies the bracket with d(x,t). Smooth finite products and sums of F002 and F003 also show e and d are C∞ on U. Record F004: the displayed HasDerivAt identity with derivative d, and C∞ regularity of e,d.

The spatial derivative identities for ubar, Psp and V are their definitions; F002 and F003 verify that they are genuine derivatives at positive times. Combining F001–F004 proves all regularity, mixed-derivative and energy-derivative clauses. Since x,t,j,k were arbitrary, close their quantifiers. The identified Laplacian is exactly L=∑_j Ssp(j), and the identified density and measure give the original total energy expression E without any change of coefficient. This proves the full exported representation and smooth-calculus assertion.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. The inequalities 0<t0/2<3t0/2 allow H006 to choose compact C such that u=q off C throughout J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Put I=(t0/2,3t0/2). All times of J are positive, so the definition of ubar gives the same equality for ubar. In particular t0∈I. Record F001: C is compact and ubar=q on Cᶜ×J.

A compact subset C of the Hausdorff finite-dimensional space is closed. Thus O=Cᶜ×I is open. At each arbitrary p∈O the equality in F001 holds on a whole neighborhood: ubar is locally the constant q. Apply M007 to ubar and that constant on this neighborhood. The constant has zero derivative (its increments are zero), so D ubar(p)=0. This holds at every point of O. Reapply M007 to this derivative map and the zero map at every point of O; its derivative is again zero. Induction on the positive derivative order now gives every such derivative zero on O. The first-order case is established. For the step fix an arbitrary positive natural order ell and temporarily assume L1: the order-ell derivative map is zero throughout O. Then each point has a neighborhood on which that map is the constant zero, so M007 makes its next derivative zero there. Discharge L1 to obtain the induction step; natural induction gives all positive orders. Restricting the locally constant map and its derivative maps along the affine time and spatial sections, the ordinary chain rule identifies V,A,Psp,Ssp,W with the corresponding directional evaluations of the first two derivatives; their component section derivatives are the actual ones asserted in N001. Consequently V=A=Psp(j)=Ssp(j)=W(j)=0 on O for all j, and the formulas for e,d make both zero there. Record F002 with this universal vanishing conclusion.

Fix arbitrary r∈I and take the family of sections specified in the local declaration. By N001 each component section is continuous on the whole spatial space; e,d are continuous as well. Finite products, sums and dot products preserve continuity. F002 makes each of these sections zero off C. For an arbitrary section h in this family, support h⊆C. Since C is closed, its closure tsupport h is also contained in C; tsupport h is closed and hence a compact closed subset of the compact C. Apply M001 with domain Space, codomain ℝ and measure dx to h. This is a Borel real normed coordinate space; its Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets. For example a compact set is contained in some finite coordinate box, whose product Lebesgue measure is finite, and monotonicity bounds the compact set's measure. Therefore the source gives dx-integrability of every such h. Record F003: all the stated sections at r have compact topological support contained in C and are integrable.

The conclusions hold for every r∈I and every stated component, product, dot product and finite linear combination. Since t0∈I, this proves integrability of e(·,t0). The existence and vanishing conclusions depend only on the chosen slab and thus give the full exported existential support statement after closing the choice of C and the arbitrary t0. In particular every positive time has an integrable energy density. No vanishing assertion at the endpoints of J has been used.

Fix t0>0 and choose C from N002 with its full conclusions. Put I=(t0/2,3t0/2), eta=t0/4>0, Ktime=[t0−eta,t0+eta], stime=(t0−eta,t0+eta). Explicitly t0−eta=3t0/4>t0/2 and t0+eta=5t0/4<3t0/2. Thus Ktime⊂I⊂(0,∞), and stime is an open neighborhood of t0. N002 supplies vanishing of d off C for all these times, and integrability and continuity of the spatial sections e,d throughout I.

Set Kprod=C×Ktime. Compactness of C from N002 and compactness of the closed bounded real interval Ktime show that Kprod is compact. It lies in U. N001 makes d continuous on U, so its restriction is continuous on Kprod. Apply M008 to d on Kprod to obtain a real bound for |d|. Record F001: there exists a real bound on Kprod. This existence assertion is valid also for empty C.

Choose B0 from F001 and put B=max(B0,0), bnd=B·1_C. The compact subset C of the Hausdorff coordinate space is closed and hence Borel measurable. Its Lebesgue measure is finite: compactness bounds it in a finite coordinate box and dx of that box is the finite product of its side lengths. The real number B has finite extended norm. M009, with scalar value B and set C, gives IntegrableOn (constant B) C dx. M010, using measurability of C, turns this into Integrable bnd dx. Thus record F002: bnd is an integrable nonnegative bound, and |d(x,r)|≤B on C×Ktime.

For each spatial x and every r∈stime, if x∈C the compact bound in F002 gives |d(x,r)|≤B=bnd(x); if x∉C, N002 gives d(x,r)=0 and bnd(x)=0. Consequently the entire predicate ∀ r∈stime, |d(x,r)|≤bnd(x) holds for every x, and hence for dx-almost every x with a single, empty exceptional set. Separately N001 gives HasDerivAt (s↦e(x,s)) d(x,r) r for every x and every r∈stime, because all these times are positive. Thus this universal-in-r predicate also holds for dx-almost every x. N001 gives continuity of e(·,r) for r∈stime and of d(·,t0); continuous real functions on the Borel coordinate space are strongly measurable and hence ae strongly measurable. This supplies eventual measurability of e because stime is a neighborhood. N002 gives integrability of e(·,t0). Record F003 with these premises, preserving the ae-first order in both quantified hypotheses.

Apply M002 with α=Space, μ=dx, real parameter and codomain, F(r,x)=e(x,r), F'(r,x)=d(x,r), basepoint t0, neighborhood stime and bound bnd. F003 gives its neighborhood, eventual measurability, base integrability, derivative-section measurability, ae-first bound and ae-first derivative premises. F002 gives integrability of the bound. M002 concludes Integrable d(·,t0) and HasDerivAt (r↦∫ e(x,r) dx) (∫ d(x,t0) dx) t0. By the definition of E this is the desired derivative statement for the actual energy integral. N002 ensures that the integrals e defining E are finite at all positive times, so this is differentiability of the requested finite function.

The bound, compact set and time neighborhood were allowed to depend on the arbitrary t0>0. Eliminate their local choices and close the quantifier on t0 in F004. This proves the exported derivative statement; no bound over the whole half-space or assertion at zero has been added.

Fix arbitrary x and t>0. H004 and the coordinate identification in N001 give ∑_k ubar(x,r)_k²=1 for every r>0, hence on a neighborhood of t. For arbitrary k apply M004 over ℝ to ubar(x,·)_k multiplied by itself; N001 supplies its actual derivative V(x,t)_k. The square has derivative 2 ubar(x,t)_k V(x,t)_k. Differentiating the finite sum gives derivative 2 dot(ubar(x,t),V(x,t)). Since the sum agrees locally with the constant 1, its derivative is zero by locality and uniqueness of derivatives. Division by 2 yields dot(ubar,V)=0; commutativity of real multiplication yields dot(V,ubar)=0. Record F001: these two tangency identities at (x,t).

At this point take just the scalar witness a0 from H005. N001 identifies the original u_tt and Δ_xu with A and L, and u with ubar, so A(x,t)−L(x,t)=a0 ubar(x,t). By finite distributivity of dot and F001, dot(V,A−L)=dot(V,a0 ubar)=a0 dot(V,ubar)=0. Record F002: the required normality cancellation at (x,t). This uses no function selecting scalar witnesses and no derivative of the witness.

Both identities are independent of the chosen scalar's identity. Eliminate that existential choice and universally quantify the arbitrary x and positive t. F001 and F002 prove the exported tangency and cancellation identities. The optional explicit scalar formula and twice-differentiated unit constraint from the original proof are not needed by this authorized route.

Fix arbitrary t0>0,j∈Fin n,k∈Fin m. On the entire spatial space set f(x)=V(x,t0)_k, g(x)=Psp(j,x,t0)_k and v=basis(j). N001 gives their C∞ regularity as spatial sections: the affine inclusion x↦(x,t0) stays in U and smoothness is local at each point. Thus f and g are differentiable everywhere, in particular on the respective topological supports of g and f. The actual directional derivatives from N001 are Df(x)v=W(j,x,t0)_k and Dg(x)v=Ssp(j,x,t0)_k. By N002 at time t0, all three products (Df v)g, f(Dg v) and fg are continuous with compact support and integrable: they are W(j)_k Psp(j)_k, V_k Ssp(j)_k and V_k Psp(j)_k. Record F001 with these derivative and applicability facts.

Apply M003 on the finite-dimensional real space Space with its Borel structure, canonical Lebesgue additive Haar measure dx, scalar field ℝ, functions f,g and direction v. The hypotheses are F001. The conclusion is exactly ∫ V(x,t0)_k Ssp(j,x,t0)_k dx = −∫ W(j,x,t0)_k Psp(j,x,t0)_k dx. Record this scalar identity as F002.

Because k was arbitrary, F002 holds for every k∈Fin m. Sum these finitely many identities. N002 supplies integrability of each summand, so finite-sum linearity commutes integral and sum. Expanding dot gives ∫ dot(V,Ssp(j)) = −∫ dot(W(j),Psp(j)). Real multiplication commutes in each coordinate, hence dot(W(j),Psp(j))=dot(Psp(j),W(j)). Negating and rearranging gives ∫ dot(Psp(j),W(j)) = −∫ dot(V,Ssp(j)). Both integrands are integrable by N002, as are all the auxiliary products already checked. Record F003: the integration-by-parts identity at t0,j, including those integrability assertions.
Close the arbitrary j and positive t0 in F003. This is precisely the exported assertion, with the whole-space integration-by-parts identity required for the final energy calculation.

Fix arbitrary t0>0. N002 gives integrability of e(·,t0), d(·,t0), each component product V_k A_k, Psp(j)_k W(j)_k and V_k Ssp(j)_k, and their dot products and finite linear combinations. Thus every integral in the following finite calculation is well-defined and finite. N003 gives HasDerivAt E (∫ d(x,t0) dx) t0. Record F001 with this derivative statement and the integrability facts just listed.

Use F001 to distribute finite sums and real scalar factors through integrals, the definition of d, N005 for each j, and L=∑_j Ssp(j). All integrands here are evaluated at (x,t0):
∫ d = 2∫ dot(V,A) + 2∑_j ∫ dot(Psp(j),W(j))
     = 2∫ dot(V,A) − 2∑_j ∫ dot(V,Ssp(j))
     = 2∫ dot(V,A−∑_j Ssp(j))
     = 2∫ dot(V,A−L) = 0.
The penultimate algebra uses finite distributivity of dot and the integral's linearity for the integrable terms in F001. The last equality follows from the pointwise cancellation N004 at every x and positive t0, followed by the integral of the zero function. Hence the derivative value in F001 is zero. Record F002: HasDerivAt E 0 t0.

HasDerivAt E 0 t0 in F002 implies differentiability at t0 and E'(t0)=0 by the definition and uniqueness of the derivative.
